Aircraft audit, part two: real turboprop figures, one runway rule, and prices that match the metal

September 24, 2026 · By the Tailwinds team

Part one of the aircraft audit moved every propeller aircraft onto the jets’ fuel scale with a single multiplier. Part two replaces that with real numbers, aircraft by aircraft, and works through the rest of the list: runways, a cliff edge in how old aircraft arrive, and a handful of prices that made one choice obviously right or obviously wrong. All of it applies in Headwinds too.

  • Every turboprop now burns its own real figure. 29 propeller aircraft were checked individually against published fuel data. About half go up and half come down: the Dornier 228, C-46 and ATR 72F were well under their real burn, while the DC-3, C-47, Islander and Electra were over it.
  • One runway rule for every aircraft. Runway requirements had been set a few different ways over the years. 21 aircraft now follow the same rule as the rest of the catalogue. The biggest changes: the 747-400D (built for short Japanese domestic runways) drops from 9,800 to 7,500 ft, the Tu-204 from 7,200 to 5,700, and the 737-900ER rises from 5,700 to 7,100. Routes you already fly keep flying. The new figures apply when you open or reassign a route.
  • No more cliff at 50 years. A type whose production line closed 50 or more years ago arrives 20–30 years old and can only be bought. Until now, a line closed 49 years arrived at a normal used age, so the Il-18, two years short of the line, was one of the strongest aircraft in the game. Lines closed 35–49 years ago now arrive progressively older as they approach 50, which means higher maintenance from week one. They can still be leased.
  • The 747-8I costs what a nine-year-old 747-8I costs. It was priced like new metal ($190M) while arriving nine years old, so it never made sense next to the 747-400. It is now $80M ($186K a week to lease).
  • The 777-200LR matches its sibling. It came off the same line as the 777-200ER, which closed in the same year, but arrived seven years older and $37M dearer. It now arrives the same age and costs $62M, a 30% premium for 2,800 km more range. The 777-8, which replaces it, drops from $195M to $180M.
  • Two cohort fixes. The A310-300 was cheaper than the older, shorter-ranged A310-200, which made it the best return on capital in the game by a distance. It now costs $18M. The Il-96-300 was priced as if it were efficient and now costs $30M, in line with the A340-300 of the same age.
  • Era games: the A380 and 777-300ER are no longer charged twice. Their prices are kept at new-aircraft level on purpose, because at a used price they would take every long-haul trunk route. Era games were adding the new-build premium on top of that, so a new A380 in 2010 cost $762M. It now costs $305M.
  • Two more ranges corrected. The 707-320B and Tu-204 carried ranges from lighter loads than the rest of the catalogue uses. If this puts a route of yours out of reach, you’ll get the same news item and Out of range badge as last time. Reassign the route and it keeps its pricing and ramp-up.

Aircraft you already lease keep the rate you signed. Aircraft you own are valued at the new prices, so a 747-8I is worth less if you sell it and an A310-300 is worth more. Every aircraft’s current figures are in the aircraft guide.
